title: Ines and the Locker
premise: Wren Nystrom, a baker's son who bakes feelings into bread, has spent twenty years being so careful it hurts—until his teacher pairs him with Ines Varga, his nemesis since childhood, for a semester-long project on local history. Digging into the town's archives, they uncover that Ines's family once held a dangerous power over memory itself, and that Wren's carefulness was never his own choice but an inheritance of fear. As their rivalry thaws into something tender, Wren must choose between protecting the secret that keeps everyone safe and giving Ines back the memories that were taken from her. In the end, he bakes the truth into one final loaf, sacrificing his own careful life so Ines can remember who she is—and who they were to each other all along.
about_author: Sable Zhou is the pen name of a former pastry chef who left the kitchen to write stories about the things we knead into what we make. They live in a small coastal town where they still bake bread for neighbors, though never with feelings in it.

chapters.title: The Careful Loaf
chapters.summary: POV: Wren. Wren introduces his family bakery and his habit of baking emotions into bread—a gift he's spent years suppressing because strong feelings 'ruin the crumb.' Establish his suffocating carefulness. Emotional beat: quiet ache beneath routine; the reader senses he's bracing for something.

chapters.title: Assigned
chapters.summary: POV: Wren. Mr. Okafor pairs Wren with Ines Varga for the semester history project. Their history of hostility surfaces instantly—she mocks his apron flour dust, he calls her a rumor-monger. Emotional beat: dread and reluctant fascination; the trap of proximity begins closing.

chapters.title: Nemesis Arithmetic
chapters.summary: POV: Ines. We enter Ines's head for the first time: sharp, funny, secretly lonely. She catalogs every grievance against Wren and realizes she can't remember how most of them started. Emotional beat: irritation laced with unease about her own patchy childhood memories.

chapters.title: The Archive Room
chapters.summary: POV: alternating. First research session in the town archive. They find a photograph of Ines's grandmother standing outside the bakery—before it was Nystroms'. Tension sparks over whose family story gets told. Emotional beat: competitive friction hiding a shared curiosity neither will admit.

chapters.title: Bread for Bad Days
chapters.summary: POV: Wren. After Ines has a visible breakdown at school, Wren leaves a loaf on her porch without a note—the bread carries calm the way words can't. She eats it alone. Emotional beat: tenderness disguised as nothing; first crack in the wall between them.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Kept
chapters.summary: POV: Ines. Ines finds her late grandmother's locked journal, written partly in a script she can't read. The entries reference 'the taking' and 'the boy who remembers.' Emotional beat: vertigo—her missing memories may not be natural at all.

chapters.title: The Project Stops Being a Project
chapters.summary: POV: alternating. Late nights in the archive turn into real conversation: first fights, then laughter, then almost-touching. Both narrate the same evening differently, revealing how each misreads the other. Emotional beat: falling, and being terrified of it.

chapters.title: Labels
chapters.summary: POV: Wren. A classmate's cruel joke forces Wren and Ines to publicly define what they are. Wren retreats into carefulness, calling it 'just the project.' Ines walks out. Emotional beat: self-betrayal; Wren hears his own cowardice out loud.

chapters.title: The Taking
chapters.summary: POV: Ines. Deciphering the journal with Wren's help, Ines learns her family once guarded the town's collective memory—and that someone paid the Nystroms' bakery to bake forgetting into the town's bread after a tragedy. Emotional beat: horror reframing everything; the bakery is complicit.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Careful
chapters.summary: POV: Wren. Wren confronts his father, who admits the family baked away the town's grief—including pieces of Ines's childhood—to keep peace after the flood disaster. His father calls it mercy. Emotional beat: the floor drops out; Wren's whole identity was a recipe written by fear.

chapters.title: Flour and Ash
chapters.summary: POV: alternating. Wren tries to explain; Ines refuses to hear it from him. The project presentation looms. Both work separately, miserable. Emotional beat: heartbreak as consequence of inherited duty—love against duty made literal.

chapters.title: Mr. Okafor's Warning
chapters.summary: POV: Wren. The teacher reveals he assigned them together deliberately—he's an archivist's son who suspects the truth and wants it surfaced before the town's centennial seals the records forever. Time pressure crystallizes. Emotional beat: urgency; the clock starts audibly ticking.

chapters.title: The Centennial Committee
chapters.summary: POV: Ines. Ines discovers the town council plans a commemorative bread for the centennial—baked by the Nystroms—that would erase the flood from memory permanently. She realizes Wren's family is about to do it again. Emotional beat: righteous fury hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Oven
chapters.summary: POV: Wren. Wren stands in the bakery at dawn and refuses to bake the commemorative batch. His father threatens to disown him; the ovens go cold for the first time in sixty years. Emotional beat: the cost of choosing; duty and love finally face each other across the flour-dusted counter.

chapters.title: What I Remember Anyway
chapters.summary: POV: Ines. Ines reconstructs her lost childhood from fragments—journal pages, a neighbor's half-memories, the shape of grief. She finds herself in the archive photo holding a small boy's hand: young Wren. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness; they were friends before the forgetting.

chapters.title: The Recipe
chapters.summary: POV: alternating. Together they decode the original remembering-recipe hidden inside the journal's cover. It requires a baker willing to take the town's returned grief into himself. Wren volunteers without hesitation; Ines refuses to let him. Emotional beat: love as argument—each trying to be the sacrifice.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: POV: Ines. The council, tipped off, moves up the centennial bake and locks the archive. Ines breaks in to steal the evidence and is caught by the mayor—who reveals she ordered the original forgetting to protect her own family's shame. Emotional beat: power's corruption exposed; the villain was always ordinary.

chapters.title: Cold Ovens, Hot Bread
chapters.summary: POV: Wren. On centennial eve, Wren bakes the remembering-loaf alone in the dark bakery, pouring in every feeling he's suppressed for twenty years. The bread comes out wrong twice before he stops being careful. Emotional beat: surrender; craft becomes confession.

chapters.title: The Eating
chapters.summary: POV: alternating. At the centennial ceremony, they swap the commemorative bread for Wren's loaf. The town eats. Grief returns like weather—weeping in the square, accusations, embraces. Ines remembers everything, including the day she stopped speaking to Wren. Emotional beat: catharsis; truth hurts and heals in the same bite.

chapters.title: Aftertaste
chapters.summary: POV: Ines. The town reels; the mayor resigns; Wren's father, hollowed out, finally grieves his own buried losses. Ines finds Wren and gives back every angry word, then asks who he wants to be now the labels are off. Emotional beat: raw, uncertain hope; love offered without guarantee.

chapters.title: Who to Be
chapters.summary: POV: Wren. Wren answers—not with a speech but with a new sign on the bakery: honest bread, feelings included. He and Ines reopen the shop together, serving the town its own history one loaf at a time. Emotional beat: chosen identity; care redefined as courage rather than caution.

chapters.title: Ines and the Locker
chapters.summary: POV: Ines. Epilogue: Ines opens the old school locker where child-Wren once left her a friendship loaf the day before the forgetting. Inside, preserved impossibly fresh, is that last bread—and a note in eight-year-old handwriting. She brings it home to share. Emotional beat: memory kept warm; the past and future breaking bread together.
